Not sure if this is the right place to ask, but I'll ask anyway. Being interested in both functional programming and game development I've been looking for a way to combine the two. I recently came across functional reactive programming, which from what I understood is about using datatypes representing changes of values over time to keep track of states and events so that functions can simply return these changes as opposed to changing global variables.

What I'm wondering is does this type of programming require a specific language or library, or could I somehow apply it to something like SDL? Pretty much all gamedev tutorials suggest a structure where you define a bunch of variables and then start looping through functions that change them. I've been trying to find general examples on how to make a game loop out of pure functions, but (perhaps unsurprisingly) haven't found any.

It's probably not wise to double down on any particular programming paradigm. Generally speaking, some paradigms are better suited for some tasks and other paradigms are better suited for others.

The most important thing to realise is, functional programming, like OOP is syntax sugar. You really don't get any performance boost out of it compared to traditional techniques. If used unwisely, however, you can make your code more inefficient.

In the case of a game loop, functional programming is less efficient than using state. The trick is to know which paradigm is most appropriate for which problem.

The reason you haven't found any examples of a game loop out of pure functions is because nobody in their right mind is going to write entirely in a Functional paradigm. Functional programming isn't a magic bullet for all situations.

I'm writing a Reactive Game Engine presently. It's a multi-paradigm engine (including functional). If you'd like to learn more about this, I mentor people in exchange for help on my open source projects. Send me a PM if you'd like to learn / help.

I'm not looking for a performance boost, I'm just curious if it can be done.

I experimented last night by replacing all of my variables with one hash table. The whole game state is updated in one place in the code by passing the table to an update function which returns a new table based on the old table and keyboard input. This seems to work, but I have no idea how inefficient it is (I imagine very).

I believe if I could divide what I have so far into smaller functions and only pass the relevant bits between them, the performance loss wouldn't be too bad, and as a plus you would directly see from the parameters and return values of each function how all the parts of the game state are dependant on each other.

I suppose it's fine if you are doing this just to see if it can be done. There isn't any problem with playing around, (in your own non-paid time)

But you bring up another reason why not to do it this way. If you are spending more than 5 minutes to try and figure something out, you are probably doing it the hard way. Especially when there is an "obvious solution" you are ignoring.
